questions.q: Is the empty-output problem only in old translation models?
questions.a: Stahlberg and Byrne found it across all four systems they tested, an older recurrent model (an LSTM), a convolutional network and two Transformers: exact search gave empty output for 25.8% to 51.8% of sentences. The bigger Transformer had the lowest rate, so stronger models reduce it but didn't remove it there.

teach.title: How it works: what perfect search revealed

questions.q: How would you stop beam search favouring short outputs?
questions.a: Divide each candidate's log-probability by its length, or set a minimum length. Koehn and Knowles found length normalisation helped “somewhat”, with the best beam size then in the range 30–50 in almost all cases, though quality still fell for larger beams. Stahlberg and Byrne call such fixes “rather heuristic”.

teach.title: How it works: what perfect search revealed

questions.q: Then why does anyone use greedy in production?
questions.a: For short outputs with one right answer, such as a tool name or a field to extract, greedy is cheap, with no beams to keep. Given exactly the same logits it picks the same token, though a shared server's numbers can shift slightly between runs. For such outputs the gap to the best sequence is usually small (our judgement).

teach.title: How it works: what perfect search revealed

questions.q: What's the difference between a search error and a model error?
questions.a: A search error is the decoder missing the sequence the model scores highest. A model error is the model scoring a bad sequence highest, like the empty translation that topped 51.8% of sentences in Stahlberg and Byrne's exact search.

teach.title: How it works: what perfect search revealed

questions.q: Why does maximising sequence probability favour short outputs?
questions.a: A sequence's probability is the product of its token probabilities, each below 1, so every extra token shrinks it. Twenty tokens at 0.8 each multiply to about 0.0115, less than a single 0.02 chance of ending at once.

questions.q: In Koehn and Knowles's translation study, what happened as the beam got very wide, and why?
questions.a: Translation quality fell past an optimal width, mainly because wider beams found shorter translations that the model scored higher.
